packet.evaluation_question: Explain whether a falling C-reactive protein alone excludes infection or permits stopping antibiotics.

evidence.text: Do not use C-reactive protein results alone to make decisions about starting, continuing or stopping antibiotics. [2026]

Measure baseline C-reactive protein concentration when starting antibiotic treatment in babies who may have neonatal infection. Use this together with any subsequent readings to assess the likelihood of infection and response to treatment. [2021]

If continuing antibiotics for longer than 48 hours for suspected late‑onset neonatal infection despite negative blood culture, review the baby at least once every 24 hours. At each review, decide whether to stop antibiotics, taking account of: • the level of initial clinical suspicion of infection and • the baby's clinical progress and current condition and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein. [2021]

When continuing intravenous antibiotics for longer than 36 hours despite negative blood cultures, review the need for ongoing antibiotics at least once every 24 hours, taking account of: • the level of initial clinical suspicion of infection and • the baby's clinical progress and current condition and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration. [2012] 1.22 Switching to oral antibiotics

claims.text: A falling C-reactive protein (CRP) trend alone does not exclude infection or permit stopping antibiotics. Clinical decisions regarding antibiotic duration must not rely solely on CRP results.

CRP should be interpreted in the context of baseline measurements taken when antibiotic treatment was initiated, along with subsequent readings, to assess the likelihood of infection and response to treatment.
If intravenous antibiotics are continued for longer than 36 hours despite negative blood cultures, the need for ongoing antibiotics must be reviewed at least once every 24 hours.

When reviewing the need for ongoing antibiotics, clinicians must take account of the level of initial clinical suspicion of infection, the baby's clinical progress and current condition, and the levels and trends of CRP concentration.

For suspected late-onset neonatal infection where antibiotics are continued for longer than 48 hours despite negative blood culture, the baby should be reviewed at least once every 24 hours to decide whether to stop antibiotics.

Parents should be informed that antibiotic decisions are based on a combination of clinical assessment, culture results, and CRP trends, rather than a single laboratory value, to ensure safe management of potential infection.
